reconcile.connective: Commentators read the two commands as calibrated to different fools, situations, and manners of answering, not as flatly opposed rules.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the verses as flatly contradictory commands—answer, then don't answer—standing back-to-back in the same chapter.

excerpts.excerpt_text: See here the noble security of the scripture-style, which seems to contradict itself, but really does not. Wise men have need to be directed how to deal with fools; and they have never more need of wisdom than in dealing with such, to know when to keep silence and when to speak, for there may be a time for both.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: MHC names the apparent self-contradiction outright and frames the resolution as knowing when silence vs. speech is called for.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The sic et non here lying before us is easily explained; after, or according to his folly, is this second time equivalent to, as is due to his folly: decidedly and firmly rejecting it, making short work with it (returning a sharp answer), and promptly replying in a way fitted, if possible, to make him ashamed.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: KD labels the pairing 'sic et non' (yes-and-no) and resolves it by showing 'according to his folly' bears two distinct senses across v.4 and v.5.

excerpts.excerpt_text: which would at once remove the seeming contradiction in these words to the former, but then they are not a true version; indeed it is right, and must be the sense, that when a fool is answered, as it is sometimes necessary he should, that it be done in wisdom, and so as to expose his folly; he is to be answered and not answered according to different times, places, and circumstances, and manner of answering …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: GILL explicitly names 'the seeming contradiction' between the verses and resolves it via situational/manner distinctions.
